name: Social comparison bias
statement: Someone with high standing on one dimension tends to recommend the candidate who will not beat them on that dimension, whatever the group needs.
meaning: The claim is narrow and it is about recommenders, not about envy in general. Garcia, Song and Tesser argue that a person's standing is defined by the people they are compared with, so admitting a stronger rival on a prized dimension costs them something. The prediction is a reversal rather than a general preference for weak candidates. A professor known for volume of output should favour the candidate strong on prestige, and a professor known for prestige should favour the candidate strong on volume. Neither is choosing the worse applicant overall. Each is choosing the applicant whose strength sits somewhere other than their own.

origin.who: Stephen M. Garcia, Hyunjin Song and Abraham Tesser
origin.where: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
origin.note: The paper is "Tainted recommendations: The social comparison bias", received 3 June 2007 and accepted 30 June 2010. It names the effect and reports three studies, of 29, 40 and 55 participants. No pooled total appears in the paper.

evidence: Study 1 gave 29 undergraduates at a Midwestern university a scenario called "Law School Faculty". Each imagined being a Harvard professor with either the most Harvard Law Review articles, 25, or the most publications in total, 95, and chose between Prof. Jones with 75 publications including 30 in the Law Review and Prof. Smith with 100 including 20. The scenario stated that the faculty already held a full range of complementary interests, which is how the paper rules out team balance as the motive. When the participant's own strength was prestige, 69% recommended Smith, the candidate ahead on volume. When it was volume, 31% did, chi-square 4.14, p < .05. Study 2 asked for a choice the participants believed was real. Forty undergraduates answered verbal and maths questions, then got false percentile feedback, either 82nd verbal and 68th maths or 68th verbal and 82nd maths. They picked a teammate for a purported coordination exercise that involved throwing a tennis ball. The two candidates were Hardy, 95th percentile verbal and 64th maths, and Walker, 65th verbal and 94th maths. Told they were high on verbal, 74% took Walker. Told they were high on maths, 62% took Hardy, chi-square 5.1, p < .05. Neither skill bore on tennis balls, which is the paper's second argument against complementarity. The exercise never existed, and a research assistant said so when paying participants for the survey. Study 3 used 55 full-time employees of a Midwestern university, 29 women and 26 men, split between a recommendation question and a self-esteem question. Both were vignettes. Employees imagining they were the highest paid but average in decision-making power advised giving a new recruit more decision-making power, mean 3.15 on a seven-point scale where 1 favoured decision power, against 4.29 for those imagining the reverse, F(1, 25) = 4.64, p < .05. On the self-esteem item the same split appeared, 4.80 against 3.46, F(1, 26) = 8.19, p < .01. The paper reports chi-square and F values throughout, and no standardised effect size appears in its results sections.

examples.tag: Two juniors up for the same post
examples.text: A partner known in the firm for winning clients backs the applicant with the careful drafting, and a partner known for drafting backs the rainmaker. Each recommends real ability, placed safely away from the ground their own standing rests on.

An officer of a society whose reputation rests on raising funds argues for the candidate who is good at minutes and administration. The recommendation is sincere, and the strength it declines to admit is the one the officer is compared on.

A chef known for inventive menus prefers the candidate praised for speed and consistency over the one full of new ideas. Neither candidate is weak, and the one passed over is strong on exactly the dimension the kitchen judges the chef by.

replication.headline: No direct replication of the three studies was located, and the closest independent work tests when the bias shrinks rather than whether it holds.
replication.detail: Jia, Lu, Xie and Huang ran three experiments and a field study on the same question in employee referral programmes, and their deposited abstract cites Garcia and colleagues by name. It reports that supervisors show less social comparison bias than their subordinates, that self-threat accounts for the difference, and that the difference reflects the bias rather than a complementarity concern. That is a claim about a gap between two groups. Whether the subordinates in those samples showed the original effect on its own terms is not stated in the abstract, and Unpaywall and OpenAlex both record the article as closed, so the result cannot be scored as a replication in either direction. Bird analysed close to half a million transactions on a peer-to-peer lodging platform where hosts and guests both list homes, and found hosts more likely to approve requests from guests with inferior homes. Bird's abstract names anxiety about the rating the guest will leave as the mechanism, and treats shared nationality as a moderator because it makes social comparison easier. Bird cites Garcia and colleagues. The choice studied is whom to transact with rather than whom to recommend, so the paper speaks to the wider social comparison literature and not to this effect.

limits: The original rests on three samples of 29, 40 and 55. Its three recommendation tests are reported at p < .05, with statistics of 4.14, 5.1 and 4.64, and no degrees of freedom are printed for the two chi-squares. Study 3 is described as evidence from real employees, and the employees were answering a vignette that began "Imagine that you are working for a company". Its recommendation test carries 1 and 25 degrees of freedom, and the paper prints no cell sizes, so how many of the 55 supplied that comparison is not stated. Self-esteem was measured in a separate group rather than manipulated, and the authors say causal inference about the mechanism is difficult for that reason. No field study of actual hiring or academic recruitment was located. Festinger's social comparison literature is far larger than this claim and none of it tests the recommendation reversal, so its size is not support for the effect. The search on 21 September 2026 covered Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar's citation graph for the 2010 paper, which returns 64 citing works with no replication among them, the FORRT Replication Database and its FLoRA companion, downloaded from OSF and holding no row for the paper, and open-web searching for replications and preregistrations. Neither the Jia nor the Bird full text could be read, and everything above from them is read from their deposited abstracts.
misreadings: The name is used for two unrelated things. Wikipedia's article on social comparison bias defines it as the tendency to feel dislike or competitiveness towards someone perceived as superior, which descends from Festinger's social comparison theory and is not what Garcia, Song and Tesser measured. This entry covers the recommendation effect only. The second error is reading the finding as a preference for weaker people. Participants recommended candidates who outclassed them on the other dimension, and the pattern is a reversal keyed to whichever strength was theirs. A third reading treats the studies as showing what selection committees do. Two of the three used undergraduates on hypothetical or laboratory choices, the third used a vignette, and none observed a hiring decision.

sources.text: Garcia, S. M., Song, H., & Tesser, A. (2010). Tainted recommendations: The social comparison bias. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 113(2), 97-101. Re-read in full on 21 September 2026 from an archived copy of the first author's own posting; the source for every figure in the evidence section.

Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology, 89(3), 568-587. Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all record it as closed, and Wiley's own hosts returned a Cloudflare bot challenge on 21 September 2026. The design and the claim about supervisors are read from the abstract deposited with Crossref.

Published online 15 June 2024 and assigned to the July 2026 print issue, 63(5), 2068-2122. Not closed: Unpaywall and OpenAlex both record the publisher's own PDF as free to read. Every Wiley route, including the PDF, the landing page and the text-mining XML, answered a Cloudflare bot challenge on 21 September 2026, under five user agents, and no archived or repository copy was found. The transaction count and the finding on hosts are read from the abstract deposited with Crossref.
